The Yukon has produced hundreds of millions of dollars in gold and silver, and will proceed to increase that output. As a business proposition the Yukon is a good thing for Canada in this way. We have up there nothing but mineral resources and sufficient timber to carry on our mining and build houses. We have to buy everything else from other parts of Canada. We have the mineral, but you have to feed us and clothe us. In return, we have the gold and silver which we can dig up to pay for our food and supplies. All our flour, bacon, sugar and everything else in the food line, our clothing, our boots and shoes, our mining equipment, our machinery and tools have to come from other parts of Canada. These figures are impressive. The Yukon has imported and used over 300,000 tons of Canadian-made goods, and paid for them, $100,000,000 cash. We have to have your goods, and you have to have our cash. That is a home market worth having and worth keeping. Over a thousand tons of goods went into that new silver mining camp last year. They will all be used up by spring, and then we will have to get more from the manufacturers and merchants of Canada. In addition to that 300,000 tons of Canadian goods taken in there, probably a greater quantity of foreign goods was purchased, for the American west coast cities are very active in following up that trade, an example that might very well be followed by our own people. You can see at a glance what a customs revenue that importation means.
The Yukon is not a tradition or a thing of the past, it is not a played out or worked out mining camp. It was hard hit by the war, but it is coming back. It has a community of wonderful people, face to face with nature, developing the great mineral resources of the country, and their success of necessity redounds and adds to the general prosperity of Canada.

On motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding (Minister of Finance), the debate was suspended and the order for Motions called to permit of the following message from His Excellency the Governor General being presented:
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons a copy of a convention respecting commercial relations between Italy and Canada, entered into at London the 4th day of January, 1923, between His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas and His Majesty the King of Italy.
On motion of Mr. Fielding, the House reverted to the Order of the Day.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my desire to review generally the Speech from the Throne or the debate which has arisen on the Address in reply thereto. Much that has been said during the debate might, I think, properly be said at a later stage in connection with the budget. However, we must deal with some of these questions now.
Let me say that with the eloquent tributes that were paid by the three leaders to the memory of our departed comrades; with the good words of welcome offered to the new members; with the cordial congratulations offered to the member for Colchester (Mr. Putnam) and the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Rheaume) in regard to the moving and seconding of the Address, and last, but not least, with the tributes paid to the sterling Scottish character of our friend, the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke)-with all these things I would desire to associate myself.
I wish now to proceed to the subjects which I think, call for special mention on my part. First, I want to invite the attention of the House to the remarks of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) in relation to the tariff. My right hon. friend had a good deal to say about averages. Averages are often useful, but sometimes they are misleading, and I am inclined to think that in his search for averages my right hon. friend allowed himself to be misled and unconsciously helped to mislead the House so far as the impression has been conveyed that there had been no material reduction of customs duties. My right hon. friend says that the government collected $88,000,000 of customs tax on an importation of $506,000,000 as against a collection of $78,000,000 on an importation of $502,000,000 the year before. Then with some other remarks he proceeds to say:
A tariff that averaged 151 per cent up to the end of 1921 for that fiscal year, now averages . . . when the sales tax is put on at the boundary, 17.5 per cent over the whole scale.
As my right hon. friend puts it, it would almost seem that he was including the sales tax in the first year but not including it in the second. However, I think perhaps he said a little more than he intended, for I find the figures he gives with regard, to customs duty, apart from sales tax, work out the increase to 17-5 to which he has referred. But my hon. friend forgot to mention several things which are necessary to a proper under-

The Address-Mr. Fielding
standing of his averages. In the first place, he forgot to mention that in giving the figures for the calendar year it should be had in mind that, at the most, during only six months of that .year was the new tariff in application. For at least six months of the twelve on the basis of which he made his computation, the old tariff, with all its virtues-if they were virtues-was still in operation.

I did not have reference to the twelve months at all; my figures were for the first nine months of the fiscal year, from the first of April to the end of the year. I had them officially from the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend's figures were for the calendar year.
No, onlv from the first of April.

I think my right hon. friend is mistaken. He may look into that, but my impression is that the figures he gave were for the calendar year. However, that is only one point, and perhaps not the vital one. But another point is that the valuation of the goods is a very important consideration in the working out of averages. If all our duties were levied on the ad valorem principle it would be easier to make fair comparisons of averages. But a large portion of the duties is collected under the system of specific duties; we levy so many dollars or so many cents, as the case may be, per ton, per barrel, per pound, or according to whatever unit the trade is accustomed to handle. When the value of these goods varies you get a very different result in the matter of averages-a result that may easily be most misleading. For example, in the year 1911 the duty on the staple article of refined sugar, converted into ad valorem- for it is a specific duty-yielded a rate of 24 per cent and a fraction; in 1921 the duties showed an average of 13 per cent. Apparently, then, there was a great reduction of duty-24 per cent in 1911; 13 per cent odd in 1921. But in reality there was no reducton of duty-on the contrary, the sugar duties had been doubled. They were 87 cents per hundred pounds in 19'll, producing an ad valorem rate of 24 per cent; they were $2 per hundred pounds in 1922, producing an ad valorem rate of only 13 per cent. What is the explanation? When the valuation is high the specific duty works out a small percehtage, but when the valuation changes your percentage changes. Take an article costing $100. A specific duty which, converted into ad valorem, produces 25 per cent, remains the same when the same article later costs $200, but your average is reduced because it is applied to $200 instead 
of to $100. Now, all through these calculations it is necessary to observe the variations in value. We had high valuations, and the duties imposed on the basis of those valuations produced certain results. We are now passing through a time of low valuations. Prices are falling; some of us are glad, and would like to see them fall still further. But when the value of goods falls, then undoubtedly there is an apparent increase in your average rate. As a matter of fact, you may have a low average rate when your taxation is high, and you may have a high average rate when the taxation has been reduced; and so it will be found in this case. I say it is important, therefore, that in looking at this question of averages we have regard to the changes in the values. With the exception of tobacco, cigars and cigarettes, every change made in the customs tariff last year was a revision downward.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me before he goes further? Will he not admit that it was when valuations were high, and consequently the incidence of duty low, that he moved to reduce the duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The motion to reduce
the duties has been carried out.
With regard to sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not that particular item. I do not think I ever moved to reduce the duty on sugar. I did vote for a resolution that it was desirable to reduce the duties upon as many articles as possible, and we did reduce a large number, we did reduce a great many duties last year. My right hon. friend told us at one time that the reductions were microscopic and at another time that they were molecular. But I noticed that, having described them as microscopic, he turned to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) and warned him that these changes in duties were going to cause the workmen of Brantford to be idle in the streets. So my right hon. friend easily adapts himgelf to conditions.
Now, that view of matters may easily be enlarged, but I think I have said enough to show that before you treat seriously these values one needs to look into them more carefully and make an analysis-
I may say I have here the figures from the department showing the months I quoted, and the statement I made in interruption of the hon. gentleman is absolutely right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my right hon. friend say that his figures were not for the calendar
year?

The Address-Mr. Fielding
No. They were only from the first of April-the fiscal year, just as I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, even so, there would b.e three months of that year under the old tariff; is that correct?
April. May and June? No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The change was not made until the last of June.
In May.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tariff bill making effective the changes embodied in the last budget was passed, I think, on the last day of June or thereabouts.
But does the budget not take effect from the time of the making of the budget statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In some respects it would. There were many changes; but my right hon. friend must know that tariff changes do not immediately produce reductions. Increases of tariff reach the consumer very quickly, but reductions are slower to reach them. The good results of the reductions that were made in the tariff last year will become manifest from time to time. If they were not fully manifested in the short time between the date of the passing the tariff bill and the close of the calendar year, there is very much reason to believe that if we are only patient in the matter we shall find good results still following.
Now I turn to a statement made by my right hon. friend regarding an increase in the national debt. He said we increased the debt last year by $45,634,000. He will admit that In that case he did certainly refer to the calendar year. Am I not correct?
I gave the dates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now for purposes of
comparison it is always better to take the fiscal year. These statements are published from month to month and have some value, but they really ought not to be taken very much as a basis of calculation. There are periods early in the year perhaps when the revenue comes in freely and expenditure is not very large. Indeed, there have been cases where at such a -time you will show a decrease in the public debt; but it would be very unfair to assume that that represented the whole business of the year. But since my right hon. friend prefers to take the calendar year I am going to take the calendar year too.
According to his statement we increased the public debt in that year by $45,634,000; but he overlooked an important point. Of that calendar year only nine months at all events were under the fiscal control of this government. For the first three months of the year this government had no power over the finances. The right hon. gentleman and his friends made the estimates, they carried them through committee here, and carried the Supply Bill. They enacted all these things; they gave directions for the expenditure, they 'made contracts, they carried on all the business for the fiscal year, and all we had to do coming into power in mid-winter was simply to pay the bills as they came in. Down to the 1st of April the finances were controlled under the budget and tariff and policy of my right hon. friend and his friends, and for three months of the twelve at all events, this government had no particular responsibility. However, I am going to waive that.
But my right hon. friend forgot to mention something more. He forgot to mention the part that the railways played in this matter. He says that we added in that period $45,634,000 to the public debt, but he forgot to mention that in that year we provided for the railways-I have the exact sum here, but I cannot find it at the moment-

Far less than the year
before anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we added $45,000,000
to the public debt for that twelve months, for only nine months of which were the expenses under our control, may we not place it in comparison-I shall not go back to the war years-with the year 1921, when there was an addition to the public debt of $92,000,000. Then in the year 1922 there was an addition to the public debt of $81,000,000.
No, 1922 was the year I gave. The hon. gentleman was in power then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The year my hon. friend gave was the calendar year 1922, not the fiscal year I am giving now the figures for the fiscal year. In 1921 the administration of my hon. friend increased the public debt by $92,000,000, and in 1922 to the 31st of March by $81,000,000, and if we in the last year have got the increase down to $45,000,000, as compared with $92,000,000 and $81,000,000, I think it is a record we need not be ashamed of.

You did not have 22,000 miles of railway to put in shape.
The Address-Mr. Fielding

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unfortunately the 22,000 miles of railway which was willed to us is the cause of our troubles every year. Without these railway obligations we would be able easily to provide for all our public expenditure and have a balance to the good, I say that in this present year-I do not want to anticipate the budget and speak too positively-but speaking broadly, and subject to later correction, this year we shall be able, if you leave aside the railways, to provide for all the ordinary expenditure and all the capital expenditure and all the war expenditure, for everything but the railways, and have a balance of some thirty odd millions to the good. That is the amount we shall be able to show as a surplus, if you care to call it a surplus under these conditions.
Will not the hon. gentleman be good enough to say that last year on the same basis of comparison the surplus was $35,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the comparison I have given my hon. friend is correct:
Thirty-five million dollars, if you leave out the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This year we are providing $67,000,000 for the railways.
Far less than before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you separate the railways from the other expenditure we could conduct the affairs of the government this year and provide a surplus of about thirty odd million. I do not want to enter into a long discussion of who is responsible for the railways. 1 think there is a large degree of responsibility resting on my hon. friends opposite. They at all events were responsible for wishing upon us the Canadian Northern, and for taking over the Grand Trunk under conditions which have landed us in the midst of great trouble.
Does the hon. gentleman - say that his government did not authorize the construction of the Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental and that the contracts were not all made under his government?
Not in British Columbia.
That is the best part of the system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have already said that there would be differences of opinion upon that point. I do not think the Laurier gov-
ernment made any mistake when they decided to have a second transcontinental.
A third.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The time had arrived when we wanted competition, when we wanted a real transcontinental railway from ocean to ocean on British territory-and we did not have it before. The Laurier policy in that respect, in the main, was a sound one. The cost was more than was expected; we all know that. Practically every public work costs more than the original estimate. This building, under the administration of my right hon. friend, has cost twice as much as was estimated. Every public work has cost more than was expected, and nobody is going to be much alarmed about that. But I say that the Canadian Northern as a prairie enterprise was a good enterprise, and if the promoters had been content to operate it as a prairie road, utilizing other connections with the East, things would have gone much better for them and the public at large. I say that the second transcontinental was all right, but the third transcontinental railway was regrettable from every point of view. For the first stage of that, for the eastern part at all events, the Liberal government was responsible.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says, " hear, hear,' and it is true. But I want to say that the hon. gentleman and his friends were responsible for carrying it through to the Pacific coast, and incurring all the expense of mountain construction. Does he say, "hear, hear," now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say, like Mr. Mantalini, it is the "demnition total" that is the cause of the trouble with which we are dealing. The result is that for this present year of our Lord we have to provide $67,000,000 for the railways, and but for that we could come to the budget and show a surplus of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000. If we are going to have this question of debt talked of all the time, let us never forget that this debt is upon us year after year because of the railway obligations.
My hon. friends sitting in the Progressive district are very warm sympathizers as a rule with national ownership, but when they come to an expression of their views, let them

The Address-Mr. Fielding
bear in mind that national ownership may be a good thing, but like many other good things, it is rather expensive.
Will the hon. gentleman explain then why he does not get rid of national ownership and carry out the pledges of so many members of this government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot speak for anybody but myself. I do not understand that there was any pledge on the part of this government to get rid of national ownership. I have understood that some members doubted the wisdom of it, but they are all prepared to give national ownership a fair trial. That is the attitude they have assumed from the beginning towards national ownership, and that is the attitude they are assuming to-day.

If it is the right thing,
do not complain about the cost of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, there are differences of opinion as to whether a thing is the right thing or the wrong thing; men may honestly differ in that respect. What one man may think right, another thinks wrong.
I am not enamoured of national ownership myself, but I realize that we are in for it and we had better make the best of it honestly and give it a fair trial. I have grave doubts as to whether national ownership can be as successful as some hon. gentlemen would like it to be. If you advocate taking our railroads out of politics, do you know what it means? It means taking them out of the control of the people, out of the control of the people's representatives, and putting them into the hands of some irresponsible body. The idea seems to be that this parliament of Canada would be content to vote sixty, seventy or a hundred million dollars every year-turn that money over to the National Railway Board and ask them to make the expenditures. I can tell my hon. friends who are so full of national ownership that the time will come-it may come at any moment- when they will find difficulty because of this board set up between the people and the government. When that time comes the people will brush aside the board and they will come to the government, and whether you like it or not you will discover that these railroads have to be in politics, because politics is the business of the people.
Another point in connection with my hon. friend's speech. Not only did he say that we are increasing the debt but-shocking to say-we are increasing our obligation to the United States instead of getting the money at home from the Canadian people. That is based upon a fallacy which I want to dissent
at once from. The idea that you ought to get your money at home-and it is a good thing to get it at home-may be carried too far. It was a good thing during the war. When we needed money so desperately it was a good thing to appeal to the Canadian people, and we are all proud of the response that came, we are all proud of the revelation it gave us of Canada's financial strength. But that was a war effort. The war stirred the patriotism of the Canadian people; but if you were to renew the appeal to-day you would not get the same response. Now, there are several reasons why it may be wise to go abroad for your money at times. You may go abroad first for the simple plain business reason of getting it cheaper. We, for example, quite recently adopted the rule of going to our own people for our money. We offered a conversion loan of $178,000,000 among our own people. The greater part of it was taken up, but we had to pay our own people 5+ per cent, and we had to pay certain expenses,-large advertising expenses. I have not attempted to figure it out, but I am afraid the money cost a good deal more than 51 per cent. We placed $100,000,000 five per cent bonds in New York a short time ago. We sold them at a price which made the cost a little over five; I think 5.12 or 5.13 was the computed rate; and I am going to put it to cold blooded people-to Scotch people in view of what I have said about my good friend the member for Brandon-that when you get good honest money in New York for 5.12 per cent why do you want to pay nearly 6 per cent for the privilege of asking your own people for money?

The hon. member will
do me the justice to say that I introduced that with reference to the speech made by the Minister of Justice, who stated that we owed the United States so much in 1921 that we were drifting towards annexation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, my right hon.
friend did not say that.
Oh yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I have what
my right hon. friend said. What he may have had in the back of his head I do not know, but what appears on Hansard is the simple statement that we were increasing our obligations and increasing our obligations to the United States. That was our great offence.
I referred to the speech of the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend, in the speech to which I am replying, to the best

The Address-Mr. Fielding
of my knowledge, made no allusion to the Minister of Justice. However, it does not matter whether he did so or not. At all events he preferred the charge against us that we were borrowing money in the United States, that is the plain thing. I want to say it may be good policy to borrow money there simply because you get it cheaper. Another reason: Canada must' continue to be a borrowing country. A country that is only partially developed needs money for many things. We want money. Capital is necessary for our development. If you are going to lock up the surplus money we have at home in government bonds, where are you going to get the money for mortgages, farm improvements, for business enterprises, for the thousand and one things we need for the development of Canada? Therefore I say, both on the ground of economy,- having regard to the rate of interest and having regard to leaving a reasonable capital at home for the development of our country -from either of these viewpoints it is good policy at times to go abroad.
But I want to tell my right hon. friend that his practice was better than his preaching. He preaches here against borrowing money .in the United States, but in practice he and his friends borrowed in the United States and they borrowed a great deal more than we borrowed too. The Canadian government, in a period of a few years, issued in the United States securities, I think, to the amount, including ora own, of $490,000,000, and $370,000,000 of that, if my memory serves me, was issued by the Conservative government. I think they were wise in issuing those securities. We have issued $100,000,000 in one general loan, which I have described, and we issued a couple of small loans. I admit there was a little difference in the way the thing was handled. My hon. friends opposite, a few months before they went out of power, issued two guaranteed railway loans and - shocking to say-they sold them in the city of New York. My right hon. friend must remember that. He and his colleagues committed the great crime of selling in New York. That is not all; they sold in New York at a price which gave to the buyer the opportunity to make $4 on the hundred in one case and $3.50 on the hundred in the other. When we had a similar loan we sold on terms which gave the buyer a profit of 59 cents on the $100. There are at this moment about $210,000,000 of securities outstanding in New York, and about one-half of this almost was issued by the late government. So again I say to my right hon. friend that his practice was better than his preaching. 
He condemned us for borrowing money in New York but he also borrowed money in New York and I am glad he did so because I think it was a wise policy to pursue.
I notice too that my right hon. friend made a statement with regard to the sales tax which I think he ought to regret. He stated:
They have added to the revenue of the country something, I have not the exact figures, but it must run into tens of millions, by the imposition of a sales tax fifty per cent greater than the sales tax they found when they came into power. That is 'a tax that is placed upon the backs of everybody in this Dominion. All who use the necessities of life must pay their share of the sales tax.
It would have been inconvenient if I had asked my right hon. friend to mention what are the necessities of life which are paying this sales tax-he might have difficulty in doing so. I am going to weary the House a little by giving a list of the exemptions from the sales tax, and it is fair to say that these exemptions, in the first instance, were given by his own government. All we did was to increase the volume of the tax-as we had to, and I am going to speak of that again-and we increased the exemptions. We are told by my right hon. friend that we have imposed on the people of this country tremendous burdens that bear on the necessaries of life. Will the House bear with me for a few minutes while I read the list of exemptions. I think it is just as well to publish the list. It is one of those things buried in public documents, and not very easily understood by the public generally.
Provided aiso that the taxes specified in this section shall not apply to sales or importations of:-
Bread; flour, including self raising Hour, oatmeal, rolled oats and commeal; rolled wheat, buckwheat meal and pea meal; animals living; live poultry; meats and poultry, fresh; milk including buttermilk, condensed milk, evaporated milk, and powdered milk; cream; butter; cheese; oleomargarine, margarine, but-terine or other substitutes for butter; lard, lard compound and similar substances, made from animal or vegetable stearine or oils; eggs; vegetables, fruits, grains and seeds in their natural state; bran, shorts, middlings, alfalfa meal; oil cake, oil cake meal; grains mixed or crushed for cattle or poultry feed; hay, straw; hops; nursery stockand so on. I will not read the whole list, it would take me ten minutes to do it. Practically all the necessities of life, including fuel and feed, are exempt from the sales tax. Yet my right hon. friend, in a moment of weakness, said that the taxes on the necessities of life under the sales tax, are breaking the backs of the poor people.

With my hon. friend's experience in the House, I do not think he should mis-state what I said. I said that everyone who used the necessaries of life paid

The Address-Mr. Fielding
his share of the sales tax. Those words are strictly and literally true. All necessities of life are not taxed. Those who use the necessities must pay their share of the tax. Clothing is a necessary of life and it is taxed, and many other necessaries of life are taxed. My words are strictly true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am going to take what Hansard says on the subject. It is a misfortune for some of us that we have a Hansard.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Outside of parliament, when some unhappy public man has said some foolish thing he can afterwards blame it on the reporter. We cannot do that here. We have to be held responsible for our words. Referring to Hansard I see what he said was-
That is a tax which is placed upon the backs of everybody in this Dominion.
The word "everybody" includes himself and myself.
All who use the necessities of life must pay their share of the sales tax.
Hear hear. Is not that true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend seems to enjoy jt so much I am going to give him the pleasure of listening to it again. He said:
That is a tax which is placed upon the backs of everybody in this Dominion.
He used the word "all" in one case and "everybody" in the next case. You cannot use any two more comprehensive words in the English language. He said:
That is a tax which is placed on the backs of everybody in this Dominion. All who use the necessities of life must pay their share of the sales tax.
Is that not true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have read a long list and my hon. friend will almost tempt me to read the whole of it now, but no, I will not do it. Nearly all the foodstuffs, light, fuel and practically what was broadly speaking called the necessities of life are free from the sales tax.'
I stated that everybody paid his share of the tax. Will the hon. minister tell me of one individual who does not pay his share of the sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All who use the necessities of life must pay this tax. I say that all who use the necessities in the case of the articles I mention pay no tax.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are the three things that I particularly desired to draw attention to. First, my hon. friend's remarks on the tariff, and secondly-
What remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the increase of trade, and the horrible crime we committed when we borrowed money in the United States.
Will the hon. member be good enough to read my statement where I said it was a crime, or where I criticised it at all? I have looked up Hansard and I do not see it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member said distinctly "They have increased the obligations of the country"-
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
"-and they have done it by increasing their obligation in the United
States."
That is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely, that is a compliment if he puts it that way. Was he contemplating moving a vote of confidence in us for doing it? Are we to take all the other statements in his long speech in a Pickwickian sense?

No, in the sense I made them. I said they had increased our obligations to the United States. That is absolutely a fact. Why does he read into it a criticism on account of going to the United States instead of going into Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What was the object of saying it if it were not by way of criticism?

I stated the object a
moment ago.
Order, order.
I will not allow the hon. member to read anything into my speech. He can take any sentence from beginning -to end and he will fail to prove it incorrect, just as he failed a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must confess that
when I made that remark it never occurred to me that my hon. friend all the time was making these statements as a compliment. I thought he was delivering a criticism of our action.
So I was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I see now it is a mistake. He said we were doing all these things, and he meant them all in a Pickwickian
The Address-Mr. Fielding

sense, and probably that being the case it is hardly fair that I should take them seriously, but I have been paying him the compliment of believing he was serious.
I want to say a few words regarding the two amendments which have been submitted to the House. The general sentiment contained in these two motions is largely of a sound, sane and sensible character. In its proper place, much that is contained in these amendments-in their general sentiment rather than in their exact words-we might be able to subscribe to. Much that may be said at the proper time, in its proper place, with approval cannot win approval when it is said in'the wrong place. The hon. members who have moved these resolutions have, I think, made a mistake as to the time and place of moving them. They are the best judges of that. The resolution of my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey) follows largely a resolution moved in the interests of the Liberal party in the House several years ago.
Two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to remind
my hon. friend that there was another motion made by the Liberal party at a later date which he would do better to take as a model if he wants to take a model. In the year 1921, which was the last year of opposition, the year preceding that in which the Liberal party came into its inheritance, we moved a resolution in the House, and I am going to read it, because that is the resolution on which we appealed to the country. We went to the country in the period following the adoption of that resolution, and not only did we of the Liberal side vote for it, but my hon. friends of the Progressive party who were then in the House did us the honour of voting for it also. It recites in general terms what we supposed to be the condition of the country. I think perhaps I had better read the whole of it. It reads:
That, while recognizing that existing financial requirements of the Dominion demand the maintenance of a customs tariff, the House is unable to concur in the declarations by the government that the tariff should be based, on the principle of protection; the tariff is a tax, and the aim of legislation should be to make taxation as light as circumstances will permit;
That the aim of the fiscal policy of Canada should be the encouragement of industries based on the natural resources of the country, the development of which may reasonably be expected to create healthy enterprises. giving promise of enduring success;
*" That such changes should be made in the customs duties as may be expected to reduce the cost of living, and to reduce also the cost of implements of production required for the efficient development of the natural resources of the Dominion.
Now comes a paragraph to which I desire to invite attention and which had escaped (Mr. Fielding.]
the attention of my hon. friend from Springfield when he prepared his amendment. If he had had the resolution of 1921 before him he would have noticed this very important last winding up clause, and you know the last clause, like the postcript of a lady's letter, is the most important thing. That clause reads:
That while keeping this aim clearly in mind, the House recognizes that in any readjustment of the tariff that may take place regard must be had to existing conditions of trade and changes made in such a manner as will cause the least possible disturbance of business.
The policy set forth in that resolution was the policy adopted by this government. It was adopted and carried out in the budget of last year, and it will be the policy we will keep in mind where circumstances will permit. I am sorry to find my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has tried to convey the impression that the reductions that were made were of no importance. I showed you a moment ago that there were stages in the debate when he thought they were important. There were considerable reductions, which, if looked upon in a fair manner, would, I think, entitle this government to a large measure of credit. With the exception of the duties on tobacco, cigars and cigarettes every item in that long list of changes was a revision downwards. It is important to note that. Shall we have further reduction? That is a question upon which I am going to have an open mind, and I am going to advise all others to have one.
With regard to the tariff problem to-day, especially when we consider what is going on in the neighbouring republic, there are conditions which are going to present the tariff question to us as a matter of more than ordinary difficulty. Therefore, I think every man in this House will be wise if he maintains upon this question an open mind. For myself, it is my desire to approach the question with an open mind, ready to hear everything that can be said for or against reduction, and then to come .to the House and give the matter the best judgment that I can. I think there never was a time when it was more important that we should realize the truth of that remark attributed, I think, to an American statesman, that I have quoted more than once-[DOT]" It is a condition and not a theory that confronts us." There are in the life of Canada to-day conditions which are not to be disposed of by any mere reference to theory or to what A, B or C may have said at some time or another. There are difficult conditions, in the handling of the tariff, more difficult, more serious, probably, than we have had in former times. So I ask

The Address-Mr. Fielding
hon. members to agree with me that this is not the proper time to consider them, and when the proper time comes, we will give hon. gentlemen opposite an opportunity to bring forward these motions if they so desire.
So far the only thing that we have been able to present to the House in the way of tariff proposals is the treaty with France. I am not magnifying its importance; but whatever change it makes, it is a reduction of the tariff, and, therefore, it is a carrying out of a promise. There is set forth in that treaty a long list of articles with regard to which we provide that the intermediate tariff will govern, subject to a discount of ten per cent on the duty that would be collected. In the case of a duty of 30 per cent, supposing $30 were due and you take off 10 per cent, you reduce the duty to $27. On another list, not so long, but very comprehensive, there is provision for a discount of 15 per cent. Therefore, even this session we are acting in line with that resolution by trying to reduce the duties where we find it possible to do so.
My hon. friends who have moved these resolutions have, I think, failed to understand the gravity of the position that is presented. There are times and subjects upon which a government can well afford to accept suggestions from any quarter, because none of us has a monopoly of wisdom. On a thousand questions that may come up in the House any sensible government is aware that it may learn from members who may be opposed to it; and so in cases of a minor character, the government is willing to receive suggestions and amendments, and even on the critical question of a motion for supply there are cases where a government may, without humiliation, accept amendments. Those are cases which are provided for according to our constitution. But I cannot conceive-and I think such a case would be rare -of a self-respecting government which is prepared to accept any amendment on a motion for an Address in reply to the Speech of His Excellency the Governor General. What is the motion before the House? It is a simple resolution, politely acknowledging the Speech which His Excellency has kindly addressed to this House and giving him an assurance that whatever matters are brought before us will receive our respectful consideration. Are there any fireworks in that, any dynamite in that, any alarm in that, anything that any member in the House cannot properly vote for without any amendment? The first duty of the government is to provide that the Address to His Excellency shall pass, and things which would be accepted on their merits at another time cannot be
accepted then. I say at once, I do not believe you will find a case, certainly not in our Canadian political history, where any government has accepted amendments of that land on a motion to pass an Address to His Excellency. I think the hon. gentlemen who moved these resolutions have acted hastily- I am not presuming to judge them-for several reasons. I think they are not taking the best opportunity of discussing these things. There is a time and a place for everything, and the time for discussing the questions which they have raised would be in the budget debate, much better, I think, for them and much better for all concerned. But of that they must themselves judge.
What do these resolutions call for? Economy and tariff reduction. Lower tariff, economy- these are fine sentiments. We all recognize the desirability of economy. Last year I had occasion, to point out the different angles from which the question of economy is viewed. I pointed out that sometimes an hon. member is found advocating economy in loud tones, and then coming in and wanting a large expenditure in his particular constituency. My hon. friends of the Progressive party are only human after all; they are not free from that little weakness. They proclaim they want economy, and at the same time they tell us they want large expenditures on terminal elevators at Montreal and Vancouver. These cost money. How are you going to have economy if you are going to build them? Then we had the charge of increasing the public debt. My hon. friends of the Progressive party talk about economy. They are sincere; they want economy; but there is a motion on the order paper for an expenditure at once to finish the Hudson Bay railway. They are only human like the rest of us.
That would be an economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Some years ago when I was campaigning with the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Ontario, I passed through a little country town where they paid us the compliment of putting up a quantity of decorations. On one which was set across the street I read this motto, which I have never forgotten : " Wise expenditure is true economy." That is sound. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) gave us some splendid illustrations this afternoon; but when hon. gentlemen ask for these expenditures, how can they be regarded as consistent if they vote for this resolution condemning an increase of the national debt? How can you reduce your national debt if you are going to carry on all these things?

9S

The Address-Mr. Fielding

Building the Hudson
Bay railway is not really an expenditure; it is an investment. We contend that it will pay for itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it is an investment, my hon. friend says. My hon. friend reminds me of a chap in our boyhood days who had a pitch and toss arrangement. He would cry: " Come up, boys, it is not your money we want, it's your patronage."

All we have been
getting so far from the government is promises, instead of patronage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is hard to please. We have given him large and numerous reductions in answer to his demands for them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And notwithstanding his vote against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He did not mean to vote against them in detail. He only voted against them in their totality, which he thought was a different thing. I am not saying that everything has been done that everybody has asked. Few of us get all we want in this wicked world, but I think it would be well for us that we should express appreciation of what we do get. We may well be thankful even for small mercies, coupled with the expectation of better things to come.
Let us not be afraid of the debt. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton treated that this afternoon in a very serious way. Canada is a country requiring a great deal of development; we are not a new country, but we are still a partially developed country, and if we are to meet the demands arising in all parts of the country, I do not hesitate to say that you cannot reduce the public debt at the present time. I take the responsibility of saying that. The late government-and I am not throwing any rocks at them-had to increase the public debt by $92,000,000 one year, the next year by $81,000,000, apart from war matters, and we confess that we shall have to increase the debt this year largely, though not to quite as large an amount. It is folly to pretend, in these pressing times of development and great needs, that you can carry on the business of the country without any increase of the public debt. Such a thing is an ideal to have in mind; we are all the better to have such ideals and to strive for them, even if we cannot reach them, and it is the duty of any Minister of Finance to make an earnest effort to see that the national debt is not increased more than is necessary. The figures which I have given you will, I think,

show that we are acting on that principle. If we had to be afraid of somebody coming every year and saying: "Oh, you are increasing the public debt," then we would be at a standstill. This is a new country. This is a live, go-ahead country. New problems are arising.
New occasions teach new duties;
Time makes ancient good uncouth;
They must upward still, and onward,
Who would keep abreast of truth.
There are things to be done in Canada, and I hope and trust the government will have courage to do them, in the belief that wise expenditure is true economy.
There is a more serious side to these amendments. I was amazed to find my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) say that this is not a vote of want of confidence. It is an extraordinary idea for my hon. friend to entertain. I want to tell him and all others that, as I said before, while there are many questions upon which a government may properly invite and welcome suggestions, when you come to a matter of passing this simple, respectful Address to His Excellency the Governor General, there can be no compromise, and I say again that no self-respecting government will stand and accept an amendment anything like that. When all these things are considered, I hope that the hon. gentlemen who moved these resolutions under the impression that they do not involve want of confidence will accept my statement when I say frankly and sincerely that they do involve a vote of non-confidence, with all the consequences that may arise therefrom.
This much is clear, Mr. Speaker. If this government does not possess the confidence of this House and of the country, there is no other group in this House that can. That much will be admitted. So if either of these motions should pass, it would impose consequences upon this government of the gravest character. Are we to have political chaos in this country? Are we to have political conditions such as may be found in some of the turbulent states of Europe where governments rise and fall, and come and go, and their supporters fight each other on the floors of their legislative chambers, and do such other things as bring parliamentary institutions into contempt? No. This is:-[DOT]
A land of settled government,
A land of just and old renown,
Where Freedom slowly broadens down From precedent to precedent.
And precedent tells us that we cannot accept these amendments. If my hon. friends on futher reflection think it is their duty to move

The Address-Mr. Bancroft
them, it is not for me to find fault. I hope they will see their mistake and withdraw them. Again I say, if these amendments are carried, there is one course open to the government. You will produce a condition of political chaos in Canada which is not good for the Conservative party, which is not good for the Progressive party, which is not good for the Liberal party, and which is not good for the state. But, whatever the consequence of this may be, this self-respecting government cannot accept the amendments referred to.
On motion of Mr. Bancroft the debate was adjourned.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the House adjourns, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. Mr. Fielding.
That on Wednesday, the seventh instant, and subsequent Wednesdays to the end of the session, the House will meet at three o'clock in the afternoon.
That is instead of two o'clock as the Rules at present prescribe. I have spoken to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and neither of those hon. gentlemen will take exception to the government moving this motion if it assumes responsibility for so doing.
Under ordinary circumstances, according to the Rules, I would have to ask the right hon. gentleman to give two days' notice, but by unanimous consent the motion may be put.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 6.15 p.m.
Wednesday, February 7, 1923.
